clue.text: TV performer in programme on plane crash

indicators.note: in an across clue, one piece placed on another comes after it
a crash wrecks the plane, so its letters are smashed into a new order

parts.note: a programme of items is a list

explanation.surface: A television presenter appears in a show about an air disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is only a link word here; 'crash' is the anagram signal, and 'on' places the programme word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of a quiz or discussion panel on television is a performer in the show.

clue.text: My polite request partially granted by commuter

definitions.text: My polite request partially granted by commuter

parts.words: My polite request partially granted by commuter
parts.note: a courteous way of asking to be excused, read also as what a prisoner asks for: someone who commutes a sentence grants only part of a full release

explanation.surface: A train passenger half-accepts a courteous plea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'commuter' looks like a rail passenger, but here it is one who commutes a sentence, which is a partial remission of punishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a polite apology or request to pass, and also a plea for forgiveness that a commuting authority only half grants.

clue.text: Stars seen in Eastern county, rising

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Avon was an English county from 1974 to 1996

explanation.surface: Celestial bodies are observed climbing in the sky over an eastern shire.
explanation.walkthrough: Avon was a county round Bristol, abolished in 1996; 'rising' turns only the county word, since the E reads the same either way.
explanation.definitionFit: Exploding stars that suddenly brighten are called novae, the plural of nova.

clue.text: What's a chap got inside trousers? Could be these

definitions.text: What's a chap got inside trousers? Could be these

indicators.note: one thing has got inside another, so the chap's name sits within the trousers

parts.note: longs is a colloquial word for long trousers
John is a typical man's name

explanation.surface: A cheeky question about what a man wears under his trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: long underwear is just what might be worn inside trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Long underpants are worn under the trousers, so they are indeed what a man may have there.

clue.text: Popular old writer with a grand manner

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular
a style was an old name for a stylus, the pointed tool for writing on wax

explanation.surface: A well-liked author of former times wrote with grandeur.
explanation.walkthrough: STYLE as a writing tool is archaic: the stylus scratched letters into wax tablets.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something lavishly or elegantly is doing it with flair and grandeur.

clue.text: Leaves space in restaurant

parts.note: tea is made from dried leaves
room means space

explanation.surface: Someone abandons a spot in an eating place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb but is a noun: tea leaves.
explanation.definitionFit: A tearoom is a small café, a kind of modest eating establishment.

clue.text: County penitentiary's wing seized by prisoners

indicators.note: something seized by captors is held among them, placing this letter within

parts.note: POWs are prisoners of war

indicators.note: a wing is an extremity, here the far end of the word penitentiary's

explanation.surface: In a jail, inmates have taken over one block of the building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wing' gives Y, the last letter of 'penitentiary', and 'seized by' puts it inside POWS. Powys is a county in Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Powys is a large rural Welsh administrative area of the kind called a shire.

clue.text: Fraud adding a minimal sum to subscription raised

parts.note: a penny, P, is the smallest sum of money

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means the word is read upwards

parts.note: dues are a membership subscription

explanation.surface: A con artist slips an extra penny into a club membership fee that has gone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raised' turns the subscription word upwards; 'a minimal sum' is the penny, the smallest coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A pseud is a pretentious person, a fake who claims learning or taste they lack.

clue.text: It sounds like an opening for attack

indicators.note: the clue says these words when spoken resemble the entry

parts.note: a way into something is an opening or entrance

explanation.surface: Something resembling a gap in the defences invites an assault.
explanation.walkthrough: WAY INTO said out loud matches WEIGH INTO.
explanation.definitionFit: To weigh into someone is to set about them vigorously, verbally or physically.

clue.text: Needing a bed? Notice outside shelter

indicators.note: one word goes outside the other, so its letters wrap round the shelter word

parts.note: to notice is to spy
lee is the sheltered side, protection from wind

explanation.surface: A tired person spots a sign posted outside a refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Notice' looks like a noun, a posted sign, but is a verb meaning to catch sight of.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone drowsy and ready for sleep would want somewhere to lie down.

clue.text: Forced to part with first instalment of rent

indicators.note: giving up the first instalment means losing the opening letter of the word

parts.note: driven means forced or compelled

explanation.surface: A tenant was compelled to hand over the first payment on their rent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like the payment but is the past participle of rend, torn apart; DRIVEN loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Riven and rent are both past participles meaning torn or split apart.

clue.text: Steadiest, flying across the Atlantic

indicators.note: flying suggests the letters are sent off in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The most stable passenger crosses the ocean by air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flying' rearranges STEADIEST.
explanation.definitionFit: Stateside means in or towards the USA, which from Britain lies over the ocean.

clue.text: Delight on account of girl

parts.note: over can mean about or because of, as in a row over money
Joy is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Someone is thrilled because of a young woman.
explanation.definitionFit: To overjoy someone is to make them extremely happy, a verb of great pleasing.

clue.text: Hold cap out, my dear fellow

indicators.note: out signals the letters are put out of place and rearranged

explanation.surface: A beggar is told to hold out his cap, addressed affectionately.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges HOLD CAP.
explanation.definitionFit: Old chap is a dated, friendly British form of address to a man, like old boy.

clue.text: Trouble caused as maiden is found with Prime Minister, initially, then a ruler

parts.note: M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over
taken as written
prime and chief both mean principal

indicators.note: initially picks out just the opening letter of the word Minister

parts.note: a king is a ruler

explanation.surface: Scandal erupts when a young woman is seen with the PM, and then with a monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prime Minister' reads as one title but splits: Prime gives CHIEF and 'initially' takes M from Minister. A maiden over in cricket bowls no runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Causing trouble deliberately, stirring up strife, is the activity of a troublemaker.

clue.text: Narrow margin of victory from leader we don't look up to?

definitions.meaning: in horse racing, a tiny winning distance, less than the length of a horse's head

definitions.text: leader we don't look up to?
definitions.meaning: a boss of small stature, read literally, whom one need not literally look up at

explanation.surface: A race is won narrowly thanks to a boss nobody respects.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is literal: a head who is short is not looked up to physically.
explanation.definitionFit: Racing results use this phrase for a winning distance smaller than the length of a horse's head.

clue.text: Important feat that produces character

definitions.note: a noun phrase in sense: a thing producing a printed letter

parts.note: key means important
a stroke is a feat, as in a stroke of genius

explanation.surface: A significant achievement builds a person's moral fibre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'character' looks like moral fibre but is a typed letter or symbol.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressing a single key on a typewriter or computer makes one letter or symbol appear.

clue.text: Like the king's wine, getting old lord drunk and sleeping?

indicators.note: getting the lord into the sleeping state puts the letters inside the bed word

parts.note: sleeping suggests being in bed

indicators.note: drunk means the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The monarch's wine leaves an elderly nobleman inebriated and asleep.
explanation.walkthrough: The old ballad Sir Patrick Spens opens with the king in Dunfermline drinking the blood-red wine. 'drunk' rearranges O and LORD as LOODR, and 'getting' puts that into BED.
explanation.definitionFit: The ballad describes the monarch's drink with this colour, deep crimson like fresh gore.

clue.text: Sweet companion not appreciated by clown

parts.note: a gooseberry is an unwanted third person tagging along with a couple
a fool is a clown or jester

explanation.surface: A jester fails to value a charming friend.
explanation.walkthrough: To play gooseberry is British slang for being the unwanted third person with a couple. 'Sweet' looks like an adjective but is a pudding.
explanation.definitionFit: A fruit fool is a cold British dessert of puréed fruit folded into cream or custard.

clue.text: Support Conservative's hidden charm

indicators.note: the abbreviation is hidden away inside the phrase for support

parts.note: to be with someone is to support them
C is the abbreviation for Conservative

explanation.surface: Backing a Tory's secret allure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hidden' puts C inside BE WITH.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewitch is to enchant or cast a spell over, the verb sense of charm.

clue.text: More outspoken as game finishes prematurely

indicators.note: stopping early means the last letter of the game's name is dropped

parts.note: rounders is a British bat-and-ball game like baseball

explanation.surface: Players become blunter when a match ends early.
explanation.walkthrough: ROUNDERS, a bat-and-ball game played in British schools, loses its final S.
explanation.definitionFit: Round can mean plain and frank, as in a round rebuke, so the comparative means franker.

clue.text: Clear bill and leave

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
to quit is to leave

explanation.surface: Someone settles an invoice and departs.
explanation.definitionFit: To acquit a defendant is to clear them of a charge.

clue.text: In musical, handle gentle air

parts.note: Cats is the Lloyd Webber musical
to paw is to handle clumsily

explanation.surface: During a stage show, someone fingers a soft tune.
explanation.walkthrough: 'air' looks like a melody beside 'musical', but it is a breeze.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors call a light breeze that ruffles calm water in patches a cat's-paw.

clue.text: Sense of duty cutting crime by a quarter

indicators.note: the letter cuts into the word, splitting it

parts.note: as in it's a crime, meaning it's a pity
E, east, is one of the four quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: A sense of obligation reduces offences by twenty-five per cent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by a quarter' reads as a fraction but gives E, a compass point, cut into PITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Piety is dutiful devotion to God or to parents and family, a reverent obligation.

clue.text: Put poem into new version for quick performance

indicators.note: turning words into a new version rearranges their letters

explanation.surface: A verse is reworked to be performed briskly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'into new version' rearranges PUT POEM.
explanation.definitionFit: Up-tempo describes music played at a fast, lively pace.

clue.text: A Chinese leader welcomed by another in Asian port

indicators.note: one being welcomed by another is taken in, so these letters go inside

parts.note: another leader, Mao Zedong of China

indicators.note: a word's leader is its opening letter

explanation.surface: One leader from China is received by a second at a harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A and C, the first letter of 'Chinese', go inside MAO.
explanation.definitionFit: Macao, or Macau, is a former Portuguese harbour territory on the south China coast.

clue.text: Appointed without any standing

parts.note: made an official without having to stand as a candidate, not merely lacking status

explanation.definitionFit: Someone put into office by nomination rather than by votes never stood for the post.

clue.text: Obtain backing for Northern Irish police chief

parts.note: OC is Officer Commanding, a military chief

indicators.note: backing means the letters run backwards

parts.note: the RUC was the Royal Ulster Constabulary

explanation.surface: Get support for the head of the Ulster police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Obtain' does not mean get here: it means exist or prevail, as a custom does. 'backing' turns RUC into CUR.
explanation.definitionFit: Obtain can mean to be prevalent or to exist, as conditions do, which is a sense of happen.

clue.text: Hot drink barber needed before journey's end

indicators.note: before places the barber's name ahead of the remaining letter

parts.note: Sweeney Todd is the fictional murderous barber

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: A barber wants a warming beverage before a trip finishes.
explanation.walkthrough: Y is the last letter of 'journey's'.
explanation.definitionFit: A toddy is a hot mix of spirits, water, sugar and spice.

clue.text: Water chestnuts here?

parts.note: chestnuts as brown horses, which are watered at a pool, not the vegetable

explanation.definitionFit: A pool in a village or farm where horses drink and are washed.
